title: Ang 642–652: Sorath ki Var
hookLine: Guru Ram Das's ballad in Sorath
tomorrow: what does a cobbler-poet dare to do to God?

cards: Dentists ask about flossing. Hymns, as a rule, don't.
But open Sorath ki Var on ang 642, Guru Ram Das's ballad in this raga, and the salok set at its start says Sorath is always beautiful, on one condition, and the condition includes your teeth.
That's yesterday's question, and today's puzzle. Why would a hymn about God bring up the inside of your mouth?

teach.b: The salok, in paraphrase: Sorath is always beautiful, if the True One lives in the mind.

teach.h: NO DIRT ON THE TEETH, NO GRUDGE.
teach.b: No dirt on the teeth, no grudge in the mind, and the True One on the tongue. Read it again as a list, and the puzzle starts to solve itself. Three places in the body: the mind, the teeth, the tongue.
All three are about what goes in and what comes out. The grudge is what the mind keeps chewing. The tongue is what you say.

teach.h: THE TEETH: THE GATE FOR WORDS.
teach.b: And the teeth sit right between the two, the gate the words pass through. Some readers hear the clean teeth as clean speech, words without spite in them; others hear honest living, not eating what isn't yours.
Either way the raga is only as beautiful as the mouth that sings it. That's how the ballad opens.
Then come Guru Ram Das's pauris, the stanzas of praise, with more saloks set beside them, the same shape you met in Vadhans.
So this ballad's first condition for a beautiful song isn't a good voice. It's no grudge.

how: Sorath ki Var is read and sung in the sangat like the Granth's other vars: each of Guru Ram Das's pauris with the saloks set beside it, in order.

games.q: you're asked to say a few words at a family dinner, and the funniest line you have is a dig at someone at the table. what fits the salok?
o: cut the dig; a beautiful song needs no grudge behind the teeth.
keep it; a joke is fine as long as people laugh.
say nothing at all, so there's no risk of a wrong word.
games.why: the opening salok makes no grudge in the mind and the True One on the tongue the condition for a beautiful Sorath.

practice: Bring to mind someone you're holding a small grudge against. On your fingers, count true, good things about them, one finger for each, even if it takes a while to find the first. Rest with your hand open for the rest of the sit.
